content: The SCO1 protein, also referred to as SCO1 homolog, mitochondrial, or cytochrome c oxidase assembly protein, is encoded by the SCO1 gene in humans. This protein is primarily localized to blood vessels, where SCO2 is minimally detectable, and to tissues with high oxidative phosphorylation activity. In muscle tissue, SCO2 expression is significantly higher than SCO1, whereas in liver tissue, SCO1 is expressed at higher levels than SCO2. Mutations in both SCO1 and SCO2 are associated with distinct clinical phenotypes and tissue-specific deficiencies in cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). The SCO1 protein is composed of 301 amino acids, has a molecular weight of approximately 8 kDa, and is a member of the SCO1/2 family. It contains three copper metal-binding sites at positions 169, 173, and 260. Additionally, it has a transit peptide, a 25-amino acid topological domain spanning positions 68–92, a 19-amino acid helical transmembrane domain spanning positions 93–111, and a 190-amino acid topological domain spanning positions 112–301 within the mitochondrial intermembrane space. Structural predictions suggest that SCO1 contains 10 beta strands, 7 helices, and 2 turns, and it functions as a single-pass membrane protein. Function Mammalian cytochrome c oxidase (COX) facilitates the transfer of reducing equivalents from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen while pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. In yeast, two related COX assembly genes, SCO1 and SCO2, enable the incorporation of subunits 1 and 2 into the holoprotein. The human SCO1 gene is homologous to the yeast SCO1 gene. SCO1 is predominantly expressed in muscle, heart, and brain tissues, which are characterized by high oxidative phosphorylation rates. It acts as a copper metallochaperone located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, playing a critical role in the maturation and stabilization of cytochrome c oxidase subunit II (MT-CO2/COX2). SCO1 also regulates copper homeostasis by controlling the localization and abundance of CTR1 and is responsible for transporting copper to the Cu(A) site on MT-CO2/COX2. Clinical Relevance Mutations in the SCO1 gene are linked to hepatic failure and encephalopathy caused by mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, also known as cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. This disorder affects the mitochondrial respiratory chain and presents with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, ranging from isolated myopathy to severe multisystem disease involving multiple tissues and organs. Clinical features include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, liver dysfunction, hypotonia, muscle weakness, exercise intolerance, developmental delay, delayed motor development, intellectual disability, and lactic acidosis. Some affected individuals experience fatal hypertrophic cardiomyopathy leading to neonatal death. A subset of patients also develops Leigh syndrome. Pathogenic SCO1 mutations have been associated with fatal infantile encephalopathy, neonatal-onset hepatic failure, and severe hepatopathy. Specific mutations, such as P174L and M294V, have been identified and implicated in these diseases and phenotypes. Additionally, mutations in SCO1 and SCO2 can result in cellular copper deficiency, which may occur independently of cytochrome c oxidase assembly defects. Model Organisms Model organisms have been utilized to study the function of SCO1. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Sco1tm1a(KOMP)Wtsi, was generated as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program, a high-throughput mutagenesis project aimed at creating and distributing animal models of disease. Male and female animals underwent a standardized phenotypic screen to assess the effects of gene deletion. Twenty-two tests were conducted on mutant mice, revealing two significant abnormalities. No homozygous mutant embryos were identified during gestation, and none survived to weaning. The remaining tests were performed on heterozygous mutant adult mice, and no additional significant abnormalities were observed in these animals. Interactions SCO1 has been shown to participate in 127 binary protein-protein interactions, including 120 co-complex interactions. It interacts with proteins such as COA6, TMEM177, COX20, COX16, COX17, WDR19, CIDEB, and UBC7. SCO1 is also found in a complex with TMEM177, COX20, COA6, MT-CO2/COX2, COX18, and SCO2.
